column4: The section’s dictionary form سَبَحَ is swimming and its race image gives it a running motion; this ayah says the sun cannot catch the moon, night does not precede day, and each “swims” in an orbit, making the ordered course itself the point rather than first arrival.
The section explicitly cites وَٱلسَّٰبِحَٰتِ سَبْحًا: Qur’an’s oath uses the same س ب ح root for runners/swimmers, giving its horse procession a direct Qur’anic counterpart.

The section’s dictionary phrase السَّابِقُ الأَوَّل places a horse first; this ayah names those “outstripping in a race” (فَٱلسَّٰبِقَٰتِ سَبْقًا), continuing 79:3’s runners and making the lead position explicit.

The section’s dictionary form أثر means coming on another’s trace; Moses says his people are “right behind me” (عَلَىٰٓ أَثَرِى) while he has hurried ahead, a literal following order like the second horse behind the leader.

The section explicitly gives the dictionary pair العُدْوَةُ الدُّنْيَا / العُدْوَةُ القُصْوَى, near and far bank; this ayah stages the two forces on those two banks, showing how الدُّنْيَا names spatial nearness as well as the near life.

The section’s wording compares preferring the near life with a race’s first arrival; this ayah names what people love as the “immediate” (ٱلْعَاجِلَةَ), making the pull of what arrives first explicit.
The section’s wording says the later life is better and longer-lasting; this ayah supplies the other half of its near/later contrast: people leave “the Hereafter” (ٱلْءَاخِرَةَ) behind.

The section’s image warns that preferring what is near misorders the outcome; this ayah describes one who wants the immediate life and hastens for it, then names Hell as the end, so speed toward the first reward is not the final win.
Against the section’s near-life preference, this ayah describes one who wills the Hereafter and strives for it as a believer; its acknowledged effort makes the later destination a course to pursue.
The section explicitly recalls this surah’s wording وَءَاثَرَ ٱلْحَيَوٰةَ ٱلدُّنْيَا: its named ء ث ر preference root and the near life occur together in the person who chooses the first life.

The section says the one behind is better and lasts longer; this ayah sets against worldly desire the person who fears standing before the Lord and restrains the self from desire, the opposite ordering of what to pursue.
This ayah names the Garden as the abode (فَإِنَّ ٱلْجَنَّةَ هِىَ ٱلْمَأْوَىٰ), giving the section’s later life a concrete destination after 79:40’s restraint.
The section’s front/rear procession becomes an explicit choice here: whoever wills may “advance or lag behind” (يَتَقَدَّمَ أَوْ يَتَأَخَّرَ), so position in the course marks a moral response.

The section itself cites وَٱلسَّٰبِقُونَ ٱلسَّٰبِقُونَ; this ayah turns the race’s “foremost” into a named human group, bringing the image of first position into the Qur’an’s account of the next life.

The section makes a race out of choosing between lives; this ayah says of the sealed drink of the righteous, “for that let competitors compete” (فَلْيَتَنَافَسِ ٱلْمُتَنَٰفِسُونَ), redirecting competition toward the lasting reward.
The section’s race corrects preference for the near life; this ayah commands, “Race toward forgiveness” (سَابِقُوٓا۟ إِلَىٰ مَغْفِرَةٍ), and a Garden, so the race is toward the later good.
Like the section’s reordering of what is worth reaching first, this ayah commands, “Race toward forgiveness” (وَسَارِعُوٓا۟ إِلَىٰ مَغْفِرَةٍ) and a Garden from the Lord.
The section’s dictionary wording السَّابِقُ الأَوَّل evokes precedence; this ayah uses فَٱسْتَبِقُوا۟ ٱلْخَيْرَٰتِ, “race toward good things,” making that precedence an active pursuit of good.
This ayah repeats فَٱسْتَبِقُوا۟ ٱلْخَيْرَٰتِ, a race toward good, then says all return to God; it joins the section’s race order to its later destination.
The section turns life choice into a race; this ayah describes the God-fearing as “racing in good deeds” (يُسَٰرِعُونَ فِى ٱلْخَيْرَٰتِ), giving the image a positive course.
This ayah likewise says the righteous “hasten in good deeds” (يُسَٰرِعُونَ فِى ٱلْخَيْرَٰتِ); it is another concrete Qur’anic use of speed to reach good rather than favor the immediate life.

The section’s running-horse image has a direct counterpart in the chargers “panting as they gallop” (وَٱلْعَادِيَٰتِ ضَبْحًا); this is a charge rather than a race, but supplies the same bodily motion.

The section’s running-horse scene continues here with sparks struck by the chargers’ hooves (فَٱلْمُورِيَٰتِ قَدْحًا); 100:1 identifies the galloping animals, while this ayah adds their forceful contact with the ground.
Following the chargers named in 100:1, this ayah adds their dawn raid (فَٱلْمُغِيرَٰتِ صُبْحًا); the racing body becomes a moving group with a destination.
The chargers’ sequence continues from 100:1; this ayah’s own action is raising a cloud of dust (فَأَثَرْنَ بِهِۦ نَقْعًا), making their passage visible.
After the gallopers of 100:1 and the dust of 100:4, this ayah says they penetrate into the midst of a gathering (فَوَسَطْنَ بِهِۦ جَمْعًا), completing the charge’s forward movement.

The section’s dictionary form سَبَحَ means swimming and its image gives it a moving course; this ayah says night, day, sun, and moon each “swim in an orbit” (كُلٌّ فِى فَلَكٍۢ يَسْبَحُونَ), extending the motion from a horse line to the heavens.
The section pictures a troop arranged in a running line; this surah opens by swearing by those “ranged in ranks” (وَٱلصَّٰٓفَّٰتِ صَفًّا), a direct formation parallel.

This ayah says each angel has a known station (مَقَامٌ مَّعْلُومٌ); 37:165 gives their own contribution as standing in ranks, so this row supplies the assigned positions behind the section’s ordered troop.
The section’s line of first and following runners has a direct formation parallel in the angels’ “standing in ranks” (وَإِنَّا لَنَحْنُ ٱلصَّآفُّونَ).

The section’s root س ب ح links movement to glorification; after the line of angels in 37:165, this ayah calls them those who glorify (ٱلْمُسَبِّحُونَ), joining ordered ranks to the root’s worship sense.
The section’s horse line is a moving order; this ayah praises believers who fight “in ranks” (صَفًّا) like a compact wall, a disciplined human formation rather than a race.
The section’s runners are measured by where they finally arrive; this ayah depicts all people presented before their Lord “in a row” (صَفًّا), transferring the line image to judgment.

The section says the dictionary sense of ص ل و can name the second horse following the first but keeps the Qur’anic prayer sense; here prayer groups alternate, and the group that has prostrated is put behind the one still serving, uniting prayer with succession.

The section’s dictionary form أثر is following someone’s track; this ayah says the heedless rush along their ancestors’ footsteps (عَلَىٰٓ ءَاثَٰرِهِمْ يُهْرَعُونَ), turning a following line into a hurried inherited course.

The section’s dictionary form أثر is another’s trail; Moses and his companion retrace their tracks (عَلَىٰٓ ءَاثَارِهِمَا قَصَصًا), a concrete reversal of forward running that shows the same following relation can turn back.

The section’s dictionary form أثر includes coming on someone’s trace; the deniers say they follow their fathers’ footsteps (عَلَىٰٓ ءَاثَارِهِم مُّقْتَدُونَ), showing the line of followers as inherited allegiance.
This ayah identifies the one who transgressed; 79:38 states the specific choice as preferring worldly life, so its own contribution is to frame that preference as the first of two opposed courses.

After the worldly-life preference named in 79:38, this ayah gives the transgressor’s destination as Hell (ٱلْجَحِيمَ هِىَ ٱلْمَأْوَىٰ), reversing the assumption that the first life’s choice secures the win.

The section orders a procession from front to rear; this ayah says God knows those who come forward and those who remain behind (ٱلْمُسْتَقْدِمِينَ ... ٱلْمُسْتَأْخِرِينَ). Its referents are disputed, so it supplies a positional parallel without identifying them as racers.

The section’s dictionary phrase السَّابِقُ الأَوَّل pairs being first with being ahead; this ayah praises the first forerunners and those who follow them in goodness, a boundary showing that precedence can be honored when it is faithfulness rather than preference for worldly life.

The section says the first arrival in this race is not the winner; this ayah provides a boundary: those who spent and fought before the Conquest are greater in rank than those after it (أَعْظَمُ دَرَجَةً), so precedence matters in this distinct context.

The section presents life as a race with differently valued destinations; this ayah says human striving takes divergent courses (إِنَّ سَعْيَكُمْ لَشَتَّىٰ), making the difference of direction explicit.

The section’s dictionary form of ي س ر describes an animal’s easy transfer of its legs; this ayah says God eases the giver and God-fearer toward ease (فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُۥ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ), while 92:5–6 identify that course’s choice.
The section’s dictionary form of ي س ر evokes easy movement; this paired ayah says the denier is eased toward hardship (فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُۥ لِلْعُسْرَىٰ), the opposite course to the ease of 92:7.

This ayah describes people who want the life of this world and its adornment; 11:16 states the consequence as having no share in the Hereafter, so this row supplies the preference the image criticizes.

After 11:15’s worldly-life pursuit, this ayah says such people will have nothing in the Hereafter (لَيْسَ لَهُمْ فِى ٱلْءَاخِرَةِ إِلَّا ٱلنَّارُ), a stark reversal of the lasting reward in the section.

The section says that being first in the near life is not the win; this ayah reserves the Hereafter home for those who do not seek exaltation or corruption on earth, a direct boundary on striving for worldly precedence.

The section compares near and later life and says the later is better; this ayah makes the choice a cultivation whose harvest differs: the Hereafter’s yield is increased, while the worldly-life seeker receives only what is allotted here.

The section turns the two lives into a race; this ayah says people compete in worldly wealth and children (وَتَفَاخُرٌ بَيْنَكُمْ وَتَكَاثُرٌ), then depicts the growth that dries and becomes debris before contrasting the Hereafter.
The section’s race exposes misdirected preference; this ayah says rivalry for increase distracts people (أَلْهَىٰكُمُ ٱلتَّكَاثُرُ), naming a worldly contest that does not secure the later prize.

This ayah says that rivalry continues until people visit the graves (حَتَّىٰ زُرْتُمُ ٱلْمَقَابِرَ); it gives 102:1’s contest its stopping point and a boundary against mistaking duration in the world for lasting success.

The section’s root ء ث ر names preferring, and its scene is a course; this ayah commands setting out, then describes people clinging to earth and preferring the worldly life to the Hereafter (ٱثَّاقَلْتُمْ إِلَى ٱلْأَرْضِ), a refusal to enter the course toward the lasting good.

The section’s image uses a horse train to make worldly preference visible; this ayah lists branded horses among the attractions of worldly life, then contrasts that adornment with the better return with God.

The section’s preference root ء ث ر names choosing one thing ahead of another; this ayah says people “bought the life of this world for the Hereafter” (ٱشْتَرَوُا۟ ٱلْحَيَوٰةَ ٱلدُّنْيَا بِٱلْءَاخِرَةِ), spelling out the cost of the wrong order.

The section affirms that the later life exists and lasts; this ayah gives the contrary claim, “there is only our worldly life” (مَا هِىَ إِلَّا حَيَاتُنَا ٱلدُّنْيَا), and attributes death to time, a boundary that makes the section’s second stage contested.

The section says the Hereafter is better than the near life; this ayah calls worldly life play and amusement and says the Hereafter is better for the God-fearing (خَيْرٌ), a direct restatement in other words.
The section says the later life outlasts the near one; this ayah calls the worldly life amusement and play but the Hereafter the true life (لَهِىَ ٱلْحَيَوَانُ), clarifying which stage endures.

The section says what follows is better and longer-lasting; this ayah calls the present life a temporary enjoyment and the Hereafter the abode of permanence (دَارُ ٱلْقَرَارِ), making duration the decisive difference.

The section says the first arrival does not decide the winner; this ayah defines the one who truly succeeds as whoever is moved away from the Fire and admitted to the Garden (فَقَدْ فَازَ), so success is judged at the later outcome.

The section’s root ب ق ي evokes the horse that keeps part of its run in reserve; this ayah contrasts what is with people and runs out with what is with God and remains (وَمَا عِندَ ٱللَّهِ بَاقٍ), making endurance explicit.
The section’s root ب ق ي names what lasts; this ayah contrasts the worldly life’s adornment with “the abiding good deeds” (وَٱلْبَٰقِيَٰتُ ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتُ), which are better in reward and hope.
The section’s wording “better and longer-lasting” is echoed by the believers’ declaration “God is better and more lasting” (وَٱللَّهُ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ), choosing God’s reward over Pharaoh’s threat.
The section says the later life is better and lasts; this ayah says what is with God is better and more lasting (خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ) than worldly enjoyment and adornment.
The section’s wording “better and longer-lasting” is repeated here: the worldly provision is enjoyment, while what is with God is better and more enduring (خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ).
The section’s claim that what lasts outlives the run is bounded by this ayah: all who are on earth pass away (كُلُّ مَنْ عَلَيْهَا فَانٍ), while 55:27 names what remains.

The section’s root ب ق ي concerns endurance; following 55:26’s passing of all on earth, this ayah says the face of the Lord remains (وَيَبْقَىٰ وَجْهُ رَبِّكَ), giving permanence a divine rather than worldly measure.
The section condemns preferring worldly life to the later one; this ayah supplies a boundary on that choice: seek the Hereafter with what God gave, yet do not forget one’s share of this world.

The section’s ordered course is not simply a contest of speed; this ayah says no community can hasten or delay its appointed term (لَا يَسْتَـْٔخِرُونَ سَاعَةً وَلَا يَسْتَقْدِمُونَ), bounding the image with a fixed end.
The section’s image gives a runner a course and an end; this ayah says the sun and moon each run to a fixed term (كُلٌّ يَجْرِى لِأَجَلٍۢ مُّسَمًّى), joining motion to an appointed duration.

The section’s dictionary sense of س ب ح connects movement with the glorification commanded in 87:1, while 87:15 names prayer; this ayah brings the senses together in birds with wings spread, each knowing its prayer and praise.

The section’s dictionary form links سَبَحَ with stars moving in their courses; this ayah commands glorification at night and at the setting of the stars (وَإِدْبَارَ ٱلنُّجُومِ), joining the praise sense to a celestial passage.
The section pictures runners with an ordered course; this ayah says the sun and moon each run to an appointed term, making their motion bounded by an endpoint.

Like the section’s course that has a leading and trailing place, this ayah describes night entering day, then says the sun and moon each run to a fixed term; its own contribution is the measured celestial course.
This ayah repeats the sun and moon running to an appointed term; it extends the section’s image of motion that has a limited course and duration.

The section’s root س ب ح develops motion and glorification, and its horse image values endurance; this ayah says the angels glorify night and day without tiring. It offers a sustained-action parallel, though it does not depict a race.

The section names ء ث ر as preferring one thing ahead of another; this ayah uses that root for people who prefer others over themselves even when needy, reversing the preference for one’s own near worldly life.

Where the section criticizes choosing one’s immediate life first, this ayah depicts people feeding the poor, orphan, and captive despite their love of the food (عَلَىٰ حُبِّهِۦ), a specific reversal of self-prioritizing desire.

The section pairs remembrance of God with prayer and develops a racing procession; this ayah calls believers to hurry to God’s remembrance and leave trade when prayer is announced (فَٱسْعَوْا۟ إِلَىٰ ذِكْرِ ٱللَّهِ), making worship the priority over immediate gain.

Immediately after the prayer priority of 62:9, this ayah says to spread through the land and seek God’s bounty once prayer ends; it bounds the section’s preference warning by showing worldly work resuming in the proper order.

The section says the later life outlasts the near one; this ayah says that on seeing the Hour people will feel they had stayed only an evening or its morning (عَشِيَّةً أَوْ ضُحَىٰهَا), sharply shrinking the worldly interval.

The section says the first arrival is not the winner and the Hereafter is better; this ayah explicitly says the Hereafter is greater in degrees and preference (أَكْبَرُ دَرَجَٰتٍ وَأَكْبَرُ تَفْضِيلًا), measuring rank beyond this life.

The section says the later life is better and more lasting; this ayah calls the worldly enjoyment little and the Hereafter better for the God-fearing, directly adding duration and value to the comparison.
The section condemns preferring the near life; this ayah says people rejoice in worldly life while its enjoyment is small beside the Hereafter, giving that preference a specific short-lived object.
The section warns of choosing the near life and neglecting the later one; this ayah describes people content with worldly life and heedless of God’s signs, with an adverse abode as their outcome.

The section’s temporal image opposes the near life to the later one; this ayah says people know the outward appearance of worldly life while heedless of the Hereafter, specifying the limited horizon of that choice.
The section says preferring worldly life leaves the later life behind; this ayah describes people deceived by worldly life who forget the meeting of that Day, a concrete form of that neglect.

After 3:14 lists horses and other worldly attractions, this ayah asks whether the audience should be told of what is better and names Gardens and God’s pleasure; its own contribution is the superior return beyond the attractions in its neighbour.

The section weighs preference for the near life against the later one; this ayah says the person seeking worldly reward receives from it, while the person seeking the Hereafter’s reward receives from it, after first setting each life within an appointed term of death.

The section warns against preferring the nearer life over what lasts; this ayah supplies a boundary by saying that with God is the reward of this world and the Hereafter, so the choice of reward is not limited to the first life.

The section’s root ب ق ي evokes what endures; this ayah tells the Prophet not to covet worldly enjoyments and says the Lord’s provision is better and more lasting (خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ), closely matching the section’s valuation.

The section’s words place the immediate life first and the Hereafter later; this ayah says people love the immediate (يُحِبُّونَ ٱلْعَاجِلَةَ) and leave a weighty Day behind them, a particularly close formulation of the section’s misordered race.

The section’s root ب ق ي names what remains and lasts; in a warning against dishonest trade this ayah says what remains from God is better (بَقِيَّتُ ٱللَّهِ خَيْرٌ لَّكُمْ), making the lasting remainder preferable to immediate gain.

The section orders a procession from what comes first to what follows; this ayah tells believers to consider what each soul has sent ahead for tomorrow (مَّا قَدَّمَتْ لِغَدٍ), turning present action toward a later reckoning.
This ayah tells the people of the right to eat and drink in satisfaction for what they sent ahead in past days; it makes the section’s temporal ordering concrete as present reward for earlier action.

This ayah describes one group asking only for worldly good and having no share in the Hereafter; 2:201 supplies the contrasting prayer for good in both lives, so this row gives the section’s wrong ordering a precise example.

In contrast to the world-only request of 2:200, this ayah asks for good in this world and the Hereafter and protection from the Fire, showing a rightly ordered desire that does not discard either life.

After the two prayers contrasted in 2:200–201, this ayah says each group has a share from what it earned; its contribution is to attach the final allotment to deeds rather than to the first request alone.
